title: Spectral fingerprint recognition of mobile signals via Rydberg atomic sensors
authors: Yi-Ming Yin, Ming-Yao Cui, Ling-Yu Du, Jin-Hang Fang, Luan-Yi Wei, Bang Liu, Li-Hua Zhang, Kai Wang, Kai-Bin Huang, Dong-Sheng Ding
abstract: Rydberg-atom sensors have emerged as a promising quantum technology for broadband radio-frequency detection owing to their intrinsic calibration, wide frequency coverage, and high sensitivity. However, their potential for intelligent identification of real-world wireless signals remains largely unexplored. Here, we demonstrate a quantum-enabled framework for mobile signal classification based on Rydberg electromagnetically induced transparency spectroscopy and deep learning. Three types of wireless emissions, including cellular voice call, Wi-Fi, and 5G signals from three commercial smartphone brands, are measured to construct a spectral-fingerprint dataset. A convolutional neural network trained on this dataset achieves an initial baseline classification accuracy of 93.44\%. To compensate for spectral drifts induced by temporal and environmental variations, a progressive fine-tuning strategy is employed to continuously adapt the pretrained model, enabling robust classification across diverse deployment scenarios. Furthermore, continuous real-time monitoring is demonstrated under dynamically varying wireless conditions, including cellular voice call, Wi-Fi, and their coexistence. The proposed system achieves an overall frame-level recognition accuracy of 87.67\% over a 60-s measurement. These results establish a pathway toward intelligent quantum radio-frequency sensing and highlight the potential of Rydberg-atom platforms for real-time wireless signal awareness and spectrum monitoring.
summary: This research proposes using Rydberg-atom sensors to create unique 'spectral fingerprints' of diverse mobile wireless signals like Wi-Fi and 5G. These quantum-derived spectra are then fed into a deep learning CNN for classification. The system shows promise for real-time, intelligent spectrum monitoring by robustly identifying signals despite environmental variations.
main_problem: The paper addresses the challenge of intelligently classifying real-world, non-stationary mobile wireless signals using quantum sensing techniques.
main_result: A quantum-enabled framework combining Rydberg-atom EIT spectroscopy and deep learning achieved an initial classification accuracy of 93.44%, demonstrating robust real-time monitoring capability.
method: The method involves mapping the time-varying RF signal spectrum onto the optical transmission spectrum via Rydberg-atom EIT, which is then processed by a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN).
model_or_system: The physical system is a Rydberg-atom sensor utilizing Electromagnetically Induced Transparency (EIT) spectroscopy. The signal is encoded by off-resonant ac Stark coupling, creating a measurable spectral fingerprint.
key_observables: The resulting EIT spectra, which serve as the 'spectral fingerprints' of the incident wireless signals.
important_parameters: The classification accuracy (e.g., 93.44% baseline, 87.67% frame-level), the use of progressive fine-tuning to combat spectral drifts, and the specific CNN architecture parameters.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes the RF field is far detuned from sensitive dipole-allowed transitions and relies on approximations like the locally stationary approximation for the Rydberg shift.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the experimental setup, the construction of spectral fingerprints by comparing signal-induced EIT spectra to a reference, and the CNN training process showing accuracy improvements.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from establishing the physical basis (Rydberg-EIT sensing of RF fields) to developing the data pipeline (fingerprint generation from multiple signals) and finally implementing and validating the machine learning classification framework, including model adaptation strategies.
why_interesting: This work directly applies advanced concepts from quantum optics (Rydberg atoms, EIT) to a practical signal processing problem, demonstrating a novel quantum sensing modality for spectrum monitoring.
